description: Composite figure of five grey-scale micrographs of fatigued Fe–Mn–Al–C steels (group is genuinely mixed: surface imaging + AFM map + TEM). (a) is a low-magnification image of the fatigued surface (optical or SEM — modality not determinable from the pixels) with a 25 µm scale bar; a white rectangle marks the area enlarged in the overlaid three-dimensional atomic force microscopy map, labelled in red text "Atom force microscopy", with lateral axes 0–20 µm (ticks at 5, 10, 15, 20) and a vertical height scale of 0 nm to 200 nm, showing a corrugated ridge-and-valley topography of parallel bands. (b) is a higher-magnification image (2 µm scale bar) annotated "Slip bands" on a set of parallel planar bands running diagonally across a grain. (c)–(e) are TEM micrographs, each with a 0.5 µm scale bar: (c) a yellow arrow marks "Dislocation Pile-up"; (d) two green lines mark "Slip Traces"; (e) a cyan arrow points to a dark straight band labelled "Stacking fault". No numeric data are plotted. The panels jointly argue that cyclic straining produces surface slip bands (a, b) and, in micro-alloyed Fe–28Mn–7Al–1C after fatigue failure at 0.4% (c, d) and 0.8% (e) strain, dislocation pile-ups, slip traces and stacking faults.

Acquisition modality (optical vs SEM) not determinable.

Higher-magnification grey-scale micrograph, 2 µm scale bar, annotated 'Slip bands' over several closely spaced parallel planar bands crossing the grain diagonally; faint additional slip lines visible in the background.

TEM micrograph, 0.5 µm scale bar, showing a straight dark band; a cyan arrow and red text 'Stacking fault' point to it; dislocations and dark precipitates/particles scattered around.

observations.observation: The AFM inset in (a) is labelled in red 'Atom force microscopy' and carries a vertical height scale from 0 nm to 200 nm and lateral axes of 0–20 µm with tick labels 5, 10, 15 and 20 (µm).
The AFM map shows a corrugated, ridge-and-valley topography consisting of parallel elongated bands, with a white arrow drawn across the mapped area.
Panel (a) has a 25 µm scale bar and a white rectangle marking the region that is magnified in the AFM inset.
Panel (b) has a 2 µm scale bar and the annotation 'Slip bands' placed on closely spaced parallel planar bands running diagonally across a grain boundary.
Panels (c), (d) and (e) each carry a 0.5 µm scale bar and are transmission electron micrographs (thin-foil grey-scale contrast, no surface relief).
Panel (c) is annotated 'Dislocation Pile-up' with a yellow arrow pointing to an array of dislocations accumulating against a boundary.
Panel (d) is annotated 'Slip Traces' with two green straight lines overlaid on planar bands crossing the grain.
Panel (e) is annotated 'Stacking fault' with a cyan arrow pointing to a straight dark band; additional dislocation lines and dark dot-like features (possibly precipitates) are visible in the matrix.
The caption states that (a) and (b) are the fatigued surface and atom force microscopy images and the slip band structure of Fe-16Mn-2Al-0.3C steel.
The caption states that (c) and (d) show deformed microstructures of micro-alloyed Fe-28Mn-7Al-1C steel after fatigue failure at 0.4% strain and (e) at 0.8% strain.
The caption prints the alloy names with broken en-dashes as 'Fee16Mne2Ale0.3C' and 'Fee28Mne7Ale1C'.

The citing text asserts that deformation twins were only displayed in the fine-grained steel (Fig. 16a and b); the pixels of (a) and (b) show slip bands and slip-band topography but no feature that is unambiguously a deformation twin, and the caption labels (a) as an AFM/surface image — the two readings are reported as given.

The citing text states that Zhao et al. [111] found micro-alloyed Fe–Mn–Al–C steels to have a longer fatigue life than non-microalloyed ones, attributed to numerous parallel deformation bands together with planar dislocations and nano-size precipitates.
No numerical values (strain amplitudes, stresses, cycles) are printed in any panel; the only numeric annotations are the scale bars and AFM axis ticks.
